Field metabolic rates under natural conditions may fluctuate substantially from this laboratory-derived maximum, yet the baseline measurement provides a critical reference point for understanding the species' daily energetic requirements. Remarkably, this value aligns closely with predictions based on body size for members of the Crocidurinae, although intraspecific variation likely exists across different populations and seasonal contexts.

The wet weight of newborn pups in this species is estimated at 0.933 grams [Wwb = 0.933 grams], a value derived from comparative data on the congener Crocidura leucodon. This relatively small neonatal mass is typical among white-toothed shrews, whose altricial young are born blind, hairless, and entirely dependent upon maternal care during the early postnatal period. The altricial neonate requires substantial maternal investment to sustain rapid growth prior to the onset of independent feeding, and the modest birth mass constrains early survival in resource-limited environments. Across the genus Crocidura, birth weights generally scale with adult female size, and the value of 0.933 grams falls within the expected range for a species whose females attain an asymptotic mass of nearly 10 grams [Wwi = nearly 10 grams], based on available records including GBIF data which document adult body weights between 4.6 and 7.7 grams. Reproductive output in this species follows a relatively modest schedule, with females producing two pups per litter [N_R_i = two pups per litter] and raising just a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year]. Following parturition, the altricial newborns undergo rapid development, with weaning occurring 22 days after birth [tx = 22 days after birth] under these same thermal conditions. The relatively short lactation period is notable given the altricial state of the young at birth and suggests a high rate of milk transfer during the suckling juvenile stage.

Maximum recorded longevity in Crocidura hildegardeae, based on data from its congener Crocidura leucodon, reaches approximately three years [am = approximately three years] when individuals are housed at a stable temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This lifespan is relatively short even by shrew standards, placing this species among the smaller, faster-lived members of the Soricidae. In the wild, actual survivorship is likely lower than this laboratory-derived maximum due to predation pressure, stochastic environmental fluctuations, and the energetic demands of reproduction. The timing of key life-history milestones, including the onset of reproductive senescence, has not been systematically documented for this species, but the low annual reproductive output suggests that females may experience a relatively narrow window of peak reproductive viability. Ultimately, the combination of a three-year lifespan and a single litter per year results in a lifetime reproductive output of approximately three litters, representing a total of six offspring under ideal conditions, a figure that underscores the species' slow-paced life history relative to other small mammals.
